name: Self-cooling solar panel
subtitle: a printed solar cell that keeps itself cool

effects.effect: cheap printable crystals turn sunlight into current almost as well as silicon
a surface that reflects sunlight and glows in infrared cools below air temperature in full sun
a one-atom sheet of carbon carries electrons extremely fast and blocks every gas

effect: cheap printable crystals turn sunlight into current almost as well as silicon
how: Printable solar crystals match silicon in the laboratory and cost a fraction as much, but on a roof they wilt: heat and damp unpick them within months, and every ten degrees of heat also shaves their output. The cover layer here is built to reflect the infrared part of sunlight the cell cannot use anyway and to glow in the band that escapes to space, holding the cell ten to twenty degrees cooler all day, while a one-atom carbon sheet beneath it keeps out the water and oxygen that do the chemical damage.
obstacle: The cooling layer must give up none of the visible light the cell lives on, and the carbon sheet must be laid pinhole-free over square metres.
why: Cooling and sealing in one cover attacks both reasons cheap solar fails outdoors.
real: Radiative-cooling layers on cells (~7-10 C drop, mostly modelling plus one preprint) and graphene moisture barriers for perovskites (95% efficiency after 100 h at 85-90% RH) exist separately; no device combining a radiative-cooling encapsulant with a graphene barrier, nor a lifetime figure for the pair, was found.
